4074-swallow-a-tale-of-the-great-trek:
H. Rider Haggard's tale of the Great Trek opens after meat is cleared away, as Suzanne is sent to bed against her will, eager to hear the men's talk. The narrator seats himself so candlelight leaves his face in shadow and falls full on the three men.

He means to tell lies about the matter at hand, and admits the cunning of his pose. The chapter, called The Sin of Vrouw Botmar, sets a story of Boer farmers, guilt, and vengeance on the South African veld. Readers who enjoy Haggard's adventure romances will find a brisk, old-fashioned tale of the trek.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amalec-amalek:
The Amalecites, or Amalekites, were traditionally among the fiercest Bedouin tribes. Genesis traces them to Amalec, son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau, hence to Abraham, an Arabian origin most modern scholars credit in substance. Nomadic and warlike, their original home lay in the desert south and southwest of Judea, stretching to Egypt's border and Mount Sinai's foot.

Their first meeting with Israel came in the wandering's first year after Egypt, breeding a hatred outlasting their extermination under King Ezechias centuries later. Entering Palestine from the east under Joshua, Israel at first fought other enemies. Saul later opened his reign with vigorous war against the Amalecites, quieting them for many years after a great defeat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-martin-:
Anton Martin Slomsek, bishop of Lavant in Styria, was a Slovenian educator born in 1800. He found Slovenian schools few, weak, and starved of books, as Austrian officials pushed foreign teachers and banned national literature for fear of Pan-Slavism. The constitution of 1848, granting national rights, gave him his opening at last.

With official sanction won after many failed attempts, he reformed the schools, writing many of the new textbooks himself. He founded a weekly paper and backed education rooted in religion and nationality alike. His priests recalled his humility, and the entry honours a bishop who rebuilt a people's schooling against an empire's suspicion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baalbek:
Baalbek, the Heliopolis of Greek and Latin, is a town at the base of the Anti-Lebanon slope. It is now in Lebanon, and the seat of a Maronite and Melchite bishop. Nothing is known of its origin, though guesses link it to Baalgad or Aven. Its monuments include three temples: the Temple of Jupiter, the Temple of the Sun, and the Temple of Venus. Earthquakes and wars have destroyed the town, yet its ruins are called the most beautiful.

The architecture and cyclopean monoliths of the Acropolis draw scientists and travelers alike. Christianity's arrival there is obscure. A doubtful life of St Eudocia names a Bishop Theodotus under Hadrian. Constantine raised a church or turned a temple into a basilica with bishop, priests, and deacons. Under Julian the Christians suffered severely. Orthodox Greeks hold a bishop there, and the British Syrian Schools run a station with a dispensary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-vince:
Vincent Kadlubek, Bishop of Cracow and Poland's early chronicler, reformed a troubled diocese and then retired to a Cistercian monastery. Born at Karnow in 1160 to a wealthy family, he studied to become Master Vincentius by 1189. He was elected bishop after Fulk's death in 1207, and was consecrated in 1208 with Innocent III's approval.

Working with Archbishop Henry of Gniezno, he visited parishes and preached reform. He aided monasteries at Sulejow, Koprzywnica, and Jedrzejow, and helped restore peace between Hungary and Poland over Galicia. Resigning in 1218, he became the first Pole to take the Cistercian habit at Jedrzejow, where he died in 1223. His four-book Chronicle, part dialogue and part personal witness, remains his great work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-week:
Holy Week runs from Palm Sunday to Easter Sunday, kept to commemorate Christ's Passion and the events leading straight to it. In Latin it is hebdomada major, or less often hebdomada sancta, and most modern languages name the stretch from Palm Sunday to Easter Day as Holy Week par excellence. Only German calls it Charwoche, seemingly the week of lamentation.

Whether reverence for these days was primitive is uncertain, though the gospels give a full record from the supper at Bethany through the entry into Jerusalem to the Crucifixion. By the close of the fourth century, reverence certainly flourished at Jerusalem, where the Pilgrimage of Aetheria describes the week's rites in detail. The entry follows Holy Week's antiquity, growth, and ceremonies across the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leopold-janau:
Leopold Janauschek (1827-1898) was a Cistercian scholar, born at Brunn in Moravia. He took the habit at Zwettl in 1846, professed in 1848, and studied at Heiligenkreuz near Vienna, where after ordination he taught history and canon law. His learned work won him Vienna's chair of ecclesiastical history in 1858. His superiors recalled him to Heiligenkreuz in 1859, where he taught until 1877.

During those years he wrote his first great work, Originum Cisterciensium Liber Primus of 1877. It covers the founding, order, and spread of Citeaux, with an account of 742 abbeys of monks founded between the late eleventh and late seventeenth centuries. Its tables show colossal labour of research. A planned second volume on nuns' houses never appeared, though he had gathered much material. His second great work, Bibliographia Bernardina of 1891, the fourth Xenia Bernardina volume, treats St. Bernard's editions and translations, essays on his life, panegyrics, biographers, inscriptions, and historians' views.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-we:
The liturgical week is the seven-day round that shaped early Christian worship, long before feasts filled the year. Jews held the week sacred through Sabbath rest and the Genesis story of creation, and first Christians kept the frame while shifting the chief day.

Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, soon replaced the Sabbath as the great weekly feast. Wednesday marked the betrayal and Friday the Passion, and early writers show Sunday also as a weekly Easter. Later the week kept its weight in the Divine Office, where the Psalter was split across seven days for prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-j-va:
Dominican Theodore van den Broek brought faith to Wisconsin's Indians and settlers. Born at Amsterdam on 5 November 1783, he died at Little Chute, Wisconsin, on 5 November 1851. He learned in Holland, was made priest in Germany in 1809, and joined the Dominicans in 1817. Alkmaar gave him a post in 1819, where he put out sermons for Sundays and feast days.

He reached Baltimore with seven fellow missionaries on 15 August 1832, went on to Cincinnati, and served at Saint Rose in Kentucky and Somerset in Ohio. Green Bay called next, and on 4 July 1834 he found just ten Catholic homes there. He finished Mazzuchelli's church and priest's house, and nursed whites and Indians through cholera with two brave sisters at his side.
hygromanteia-delatte-1927-greek:
Armand Delatte, a Belgian scholar of Greek magic, printed his Anecdota Atheniensia at Liège in 1927. Pages 397 to 445 hold the Hygromanteia, the Greek Magical Treatise of Solomon. The text is in Greek, copied from old manuscripts held in Athens.

The treatise teaches water divination and the calling of spirits tied to the planets. It lists ranks of angels and demons, and gives prayers and seals for ruling them. Older than the famous Key of Solomon, it stands near the root of the whole Solomonic grimoire line. Delatte's printing kept the work from being lost with its manuscripts.
podcast-dannyjones-L_3_D1b0WEk:
Bart Ehrman is one of the best-known scholars of the New Testament, a former believer whose textual studies led him out of his faith. With Danny Jones, the ancient religion expert discusses the secret gospels, the writings the early church excluded, and his account of where the historical Jesus can and cannot be found.

Ehrman explains how scholars date texts, spot edits, and rebuild what the first Christians actually believed before doctrine settled. Jones asks the questions his audience brings, including the conspiratorial ones, and Ehrman answers them with a teacher's patience and a skeptic's edge. Little here is fringe; the disputes are the real ones inside biblical scholarship. The episode gives listeners the mainstream critical case on Jesus and the gospels, from its most famous living presenter.
swallow-a-tale-of-the-great-trek:
H. Rider Haggard's Swallow, A Tale of the Great Trek, tells a South African story through the mouth of Vrouw Botmar, whose tale the first chapter introduces. Suzanne Botmar finds the shipwrecked Ralph Kenzie, and their love runs through the book's long chain of chapters.

The contents pass through shipwreck, the coming of Englishmen, Suzanne saving the witch-finder Sihamba, a wedding, and Ralph returning into the sea and coming back to the farm. The white swallow gives an omen, and the war of the clean spear, the madness of Ralph, and the Great Trek itself follow. Swart Piet sets a snare, an impi comes, thirst strikes, and the pass of the Quathlamba closes the trek. Haggard mixes romance with the Boer migration's hardships.
the-history-of-caliph-vathek:
William Beckford wrote The History of the Caliph Vathek, shown in the 1887 Cassell & Company edition, with a heading in the record dated 1786. An introduction gives Beckford's family history. Born in 1759, he was the son of an alderman who twice became Lord Mayor of London, and the family wealth came from plantations in Jamaica.

The introduction jokes that Vathek reads like an alderman's dream after a heavy dinner at the Mansion House. Devotion to the senses fills the tale: tables covered thirty times over for a guest, bowls of rock crystal drained without end, and nightmare events that end in a most terrible heartburn. Readers meet the author through his father's feasts and fortune first.
the-secret-of-sarek:
Maurice Leblanc's The Secret of Sarek was translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. The Macaulay Company copyrighted this edition in 1920. A foreword recalls the Hergemont scandal of seventeen years before. Few people remember it now, Leblanc warns. His foreword supplies the details in a few lines.

In July 1902, Antoine d'Hergemont walked in the Bois with his daughter Véronique. Four men assaulted him and felled him with a walking-stick blow. Véronique was dragged into a motor-car despite her struggles. Count Alexis Vorski, a young Polish nobleman, had planned the kidnapping. He loved Véronique, and she loved him. Her father had repelled and insulted him more than once. The wedding followed two months later at Nice. D'Hergemont then kidnapped the couple's child and sailed away in a small yacht, the foreword says.
the-unseen-bridegroom-or-wedded-for-a-we:
May Agnes Fleming begins her novel on a wet, windy November afternoon in New York. Sleet lashes the windows while Mrs. Walraven prepares a ball, her first in twenty years, meant to be among the season's most brilliant affairs. All Fifth Avenue is expected at her brownstone palace of velvet carpets and gilded furniture.

Mrs. Ferdinand Walraven herself is rich, arrogant, and ill-tempered, with few rivals on the avenue in any of those qualities. Her only son sits upstairs smoking cigars and staring into the rainy twilight. Fleming's opening sets wealth and gloom side by side, promising a week-long marriage plot, as the subtitle Wedded for a Week announces, inside fashionable society.
